articles.title: How a Flush Toilet Works: Cistern, Siphon and Trap
articles.excerpt: A cistern stores a set amount of water, a valve releases it in seconds and a bent pipe keeps sewer gas out. Here is each part and how it fits together.
blocks: A flush toilet works by storing a fixed amount of water in a tank, releasing it quickly into the bowl so that waste is carried away, and then refilling the tank for next time. A bend in the pipe below the bowl keeps a plug of water in place, which stops gas from the sewer coming back into the room. Almost every part of the system is mechanical and driven by gravity, which is why the basic design has changed little in well over a century.
The cistern: a measured store of water

The tank behind or above the bowl is called the cistern. Its job is to hold enough water to flush in one go. According to Wikipedia's article on the flush toilet, modern tanks hold roughly 3 to 6 litres. Because the water is released from a height, it arrives in the bowl with force, and that force is what pushes waste through the outlet.
Pressing the button or lever opens a path from the tank to the bowl. Which kind of path depends on the design, and there are two common ones.
Two ways to start a flush

The first is the **flapper** (also called a drop valve). A rubber flap covers the outlet at the bottom of the tank, and the weight of the water above presses it shut. The handle lifts the flap on a chain, the tank empties into the bowl, and the flap drops back down as the level falls. Wikipedia notes this design is common in North America and continental Europe, and that it became legal in UK homes in 2001.

The second is the **siphon**. Here there is no flap that has to seal against the water. The handle lifts a disc that forces water over the top of a bent tube. Once the tube is full, siphonic flow takes over and pulls the rest of the tank through it. The flush ends when air enters the top of the tube and breaks the flow. The same article credits Albert Giblin with this valveless system, and says UK rules required siphon cisterns until 1 January 2001.

Flapper: a rubber seal opens and closes; simple, but the seal can wear.
Siphon: no sealing washer is needed; flow stops when air enters the tube.

After the flush, a fill valve lets fresh water back into the tank. A float sits on the surface and rises with the water. When it reaches the intended level, it closes the valve. If the float or valve fails, water can keep running into the tank, which is why tanks have an overflow pipe leading to the bowl or outside.
The same article says Joseph Bramah patented a float valve for flush tanks in 1778, and that a concentric-float design, where the float surrounds the valve, dates from 1957.
The trap: why the bowl smells of nothing

Under the bowl the pipe curves into a U or S shape. Water stays in the bend after every flush, forming a seal. Sewer gas cannot pass through standing water, so it stays in the drain. Wikipedia credits Alexander Cumming with patenting the S-trap in 1775, and says Bramah later improved on his design by replacing a sliding valve with a hinged flap.

The idea is older than the patents. Sir John Harington published a description of a forerunner of the modern toilet in 1596, with a flush valve and a wash-down bowl, and installed one for Queen Elizabeth I at Richmond Palace, according to Wikipedia.

A popular legend says Thomas Crapper invented the flush toilet. The same article says plainly that this is not true. It credits him with nine patents and with popularising the siphon system for emptying the tank.

Not every flush needs the same amount of water. The company Caroma developed the Duoset cistern in Australia in 1980, with two buttons: a small flush for liquid waste and a larger one for solid waste. Wikipedia says modern versions of this design can save the average household a large share of its normal toilet water use, with a figure of 67 per cent quoted there.

Toilets matter for household water use. The US Environmental Protection Agency says toilets are the largest source of indoor water use in a home, at nearly 30 per cent of the total. The current US federal standard allows 1.6 gallons per flush, while toilets with the EPA's WaterSense label use 1.28 gallons per flush or less, about 20 per cent less. Some older models use as much as 6 gallons per flush, according to the agency.

The EPA also says that household leaks can waste up to 180 gallons a week, and that toilets are often the cause. It names worn flappers as the usual culprit. A leaking flapper lets water trickle from the tank into the bowl, so the fill valve keeps topping up the tank.
This is general information about how the parts work. Plumbing rules, flush volumes and approved designs differ between countries, and the figures above come from US and UK sources.

You press the button, and the flapper lifts or the siphon starts.
The tank water rushes into the bowl and pushes its contents through the trap.
The flush stops when the tank empties, or when air breaks the siphon.
The fill valve refills the tank until the float shuts it off.
Water left in the trap seals the drain until next time.
That sequence of store, release, seal and refill is the whole mechanism. The differences between toilet models are mostly in how the release step is done and how much water it uses.

sources.title: Residential Toilets, US Environmental Protection Agency WaterSense

articles.title: Real vs Nominal Interest Rates: What Inflation Takes Away
articles.excerpt: The rate on a deposit or loan is not the whole story. Subtract inflation to see the real return, and learn the Fisher equation with a worked example.
blocks: The nominal interest rate is the rate written on a loan or deposit. The real interest rate is what is left after inflation, and it shows how much buying power a saver gains or a borrower gives up. A 6 per cent deposit sounds good, but if prices rise 7 per cent over the same year, the saver can buy slightly less than before.
Two rates for the same money

The European Central Bank explains the nominal rate as the rate that is actually agreed and paid. A borrower pays it on a mortgage, and a saver receives it on a deposit. The real rate is the nominal rate adjusted for inflation. It tells you what happens to purchasing power, not just the number in an account.
The quick rule from the ECB's explainer is: real rate = nominal rate minus inflation.

The ECB uses a euro example. A saver puts 1,000 euros in a deposit for a year at a nominal rate of 2.5 per cent, and ends with 1,025 euros. If prices rise 3 per cent in that year, goods that cost 1,000 euros a year earlier now cost 1,030 euros. The saver is 5 euros short of the same basket, and the real return is 2.5 minus 3, which is minus 0.5 per cent.
The same logic works for any currency. Put in your own numbers:

Nominal rate: 6 per cent
Inflation over the same year: 4 per cent
Approximate real rate: 6 minus 4, which is 2 per cent

Economists link the three numbers with the Fisher equation, named after the economist Irving Fisher. Wikipedia gives its exact form as (1 + i) = (1 + r) x (1 + p), where i is the nominal rate, r is the real rate and p is inflation. Rearranged, the real rate is r = (i minus p) divided by (1 + p).

When rates and inflation are low, the simple subtraction is close enough: r is roughly i minus p. The two methods drift apart when numbers get large. Wikipedia's example is a lender who earns 10 per cent while prices rise 25 per cent. Subtraction suggests a loss of about 15 per cent, but the exact calculation, 1.10 divided by 1.25 minus 1, gives a loss of 12 per cent. The article itself calls the approximation a bit rough.

Take a nominal rate of 8 per cent and inflation of 5 per cent. Subtraction gives 3 per cent. The exact formula gives 1.08 divided by 1.05, minus 1, which is about 2.86 per cent. For everyday comparisons the gap is small, but it grows as inflation rises.
Before and after: ex-ante and ex-post
Inflation is only known once the year is over, which creates two versions of the real rate. Wikipedia describes them this way:

**Ex-ante real rate:** the rate expected when the loan or deposit is made, using expected inflation. Different people can hold different expectations.
**Ex-post real rate:** the rate known afterwards, using the inflation that actually happened.

A fixed-rate deposit has a known nominal return, but its real return is only certain in hindsight. The article notes that inflation-indexed bonds have made the market's expected real rates observable, because their payments are tied to measured inflation.
Why a positive rate can still lose value

The ECB points out that a positive nominal rate can still mean a loss in buying power when inflation is high. Its example is the early 1980s, when nominal rates in the euro area were high, but inflation was higher still, so the average real rate was low.
The reverse also holds for borrowers. When inflation is above the loan rate, the real rate is negative, and the amount repaid is worth less in goods than the amount borrowed.

The calculation depends on which price measure you choose. Most countries publish a consumer price index, and the headline figure is an average across a basket of goods. Your own spending may rise faster or slower than that average. If you want to know how the index is built, see our article on how inflation is measured.
This article explains a formula and is general information, not financial advice. It uses published examples, and real outcomes depend on actual inflation and on any tax on interest.

Nominal rate: the rate stated and paid.
Real rate: the nominal rate adjusted for inflation.
Quick estimate: subtract inflation from the nominal rate.
Exact: divide (1 + nominal) by (1 + inflation) and subtract 1.
Expected inflation gives an ex-ante rate; actual inflation gives an ex-post rate.

sources.title: Nominal and real interest rates, European Central Bank

articles.title: How ADS-B Lets Aircraft Broadcast Their Own Position
articles.excerpt: ADS-B aircraft work out their position from satellite navigation and broadcast it about once a second. See what is sent, who hears it and what limits it.
blocks: ADS-B stands for Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast. An aircraft with ADS-B works out where it is, usually from satellite navigation, and broadcasts that position automatically, around once every second. Air traffic control, other aircraft and anyone with a suitable receiver can pick it up. It is a different approach from traditional radar, which finds an aircraft by sending out a signal and waiting for the echo.

**Automatic:** the broadcast happens without a ground station asking for it.
**Dependent:** the data depends on the aircraft's own navigation equipment.
**Surveillance:** its purpose is to let others see where aircraft are.
**Broadcast:** the signal is sent to anyone listening, not to one named receiver.

Wikipedia's article on ADS-B describes it as a technology in which the aircraft determines its own position, usually from satellite navigation, and broadcasts it so that it can be tracked. SKYbrary, an aviation safety reference, quotes the ICAO definition: a means by which aircraft, aerodrome vehicles and other objects can automatically transmit and receive data.

Two things are required. One is a source of position, normally a GPS receiver or another certified satellite navigation unit. The other is the ADS-B transmitter itself, a datalink that sends the message. Unlike secondary radar, no interrogation from the ground or from another aircraft is needed. The aircraft simply transmits.
According to SKYbrary, the data includes the following:

Latitude and longitude
Barometric altitude (the height measured from air pressure)
Quality indicators, which say how good the position data is
The aircraft's identification, including its 24-bit address
Emergency status
A special position indicator, when the crew selects it
Wikipedia adds that velocity, including ground speed, is part of the broadcast, and that position and velocity are sent about once per second.
There are two main datalinks, and which is used depends on the region and type of flying.

**1090 MHz extended squitter (1090ES):** in effect a modified Mode S transponder. Existing air traffic control receivers and collision-avoidance equipment can already receive these signals. SKYbrary says it is the basis of the most widely shared global use.
**978 MHz Universal Access Transceiver (UAT):** a separate link used in the United States, mainly by general aviation. Wikipedia says it can carry weather and flight information services that 1090ES cannot, and that the US FAA has suggested aircraft staying below 18,000 feet use it to reduce crowding on 1090 MHz.
SKYbrary notes that using different datalinks in different regions limits full uniformity.

**ADS-B Out** is the sending side. Ground stations or satellite receivers collect it for surveillance. **ADS-B In** is the receiving side: an aircraft with the right equipment can see nearby traffic with altitude, heading, speed and distance. In the United States, ground services can add traffic reports from other sources and weather information. Wikipedia says ADS-B In is not mandated in US airspace.

SKYbrary explains that ground stations pass the data to processing systems, where it is combined with radar or multilateration inputs to build one picture of the traffic. One benefit it lists is lower infrastructure cost than radar. Another is surveillance coverage from gate to gate, including air-to-air coverage.

Rules differ by country. Wikipedia says that ADS-B Out has been required in most controlled airspace in the United States, including Classes A, B and C, since the compliance date of 1 January 2020. In Europe, equipment has been mandatory for some aircraft since 2017, and in Australia it is required for all aircraft flying under instrument rules, and for all aircraft at or above flight level 300. SKYbrary adds that European rules apply to instrument flight aircraft above certain weight or speed thresholds. Check current rules with the aviation authority concerned, as the details change.

Aircraft with no transponder, or only older transponder equipment, do not appear on ADS-B displays.
The system depends on onboard navigation, which can fail.
Signal reception weakens with distance, and terrain, weather or interference can stop messages being decoded.
Gliders using FLARM collision-avoidance equipment cannot see ADS-B-only aircraft, and the reverse also holds.

ADS-B messages are not encrypted, so anyone with a receiver can read them. Wikipedia reports that researchers have shown spoofed messages can create phantom aircraft, and that cross-checking against radar or multilateration is one proposed defence. Because each aircraft has a unique 24-bit address, its movements are easy to follow, and the FAA offers some privacy programmes that do not change the underlying broadcast.
This article describes the technology in general terms. Equipment standards and mandates are set by national aviation authorities and change over time.
In short, ADS-B moves the job of finding the aircraft from the ground to the aircraft itself, which then shares what it knows with everyone in range.

articles.title: How a Car Differential Lets Wheels Turn at Different Speeds
articles.excerpt: In a corner, the outer wheel travels farther than the inner one. A differential splits engine power between them. See open, limited-slip and locking types.
blocks: A differential is a set of gears that lets the two driven wheels on one axle spin at different speeds while both still receive power from the engine. It is needed because, when a car turns, the outer wheel travels farther than the inner wheel in the same time. Without a differential, one wheel would have to skid or hop through every bend.

Wheels that are not driven can turn freely and each find their own speed. Driven wheels are different, because both are connected to the engine through the same shaft. Wikipedia's article on the differential puts it simply: the outer wheels must travel farther than the inner wheels in a turn, so the drive wheels need a way to turn at different rates.
The mechanical idea is a gear train with three shafts, where the speed of one shaft is the average of the other two. In a car, the shaft from the engine feeds two output shafts, one for each wheel.

The common layout uses a ring-and-pinion pair. The pinion, a small gear on the end of the driveshaft, meshes with a large ring gear. This turns the power through 90 degrees, from the lengthwise driveshaft to the sideways axles, and since the pinion has fewer teeth than the ring gear, it also provides a gear reduction.

The ring gear carries a small set of gears inside a case. When the car goes straight, they do not turn relative to each other and both axles move at the same speed. In a corner, the outer wheel's side gear turns faster than the inner one, and the small gears rotate to let that happen while still passing on torque. Gear Patrol, a motoring site, describes the effect as the faster outside wheel's gear spinning around the slower inside gear while the car turns.
The weakness of the open design

An open differential tends to send power to whichever wheel has less grip. Wikipedia says its drawback is that the wheel with less traction can spin. Motor1 gives the same explanation: when one wheel loses grip, torque flows to it and it spins freely. On a wet or icy surface, or when one wheel is lifted, the wheel with grip may get little drive.
A limited-slip differential (LSD) restricts the difference in power sent to each wheel. Motor1 describes three common types:

**Clutch-based:** clutch packs sit behind each side gear. A spring keeps them lightly loaded in normal cornering. When one wheel starts to slip under power, the packs clamp and more torque goes to the wheel with grip.
**Torsen:** uses worm gears to direct torque to the wheel with more grip, without clutches. Wikipedia says it was patented by Vernon Gleasman in 1958.
**Viscous:** links the two outputs through a chamber of thick silicone fluid, which keeps the wheels at similar speeds.

Motor1 says Porsche first commissioned limited-slip differentials in the 1930s for its race cars. An LSD still lets the wheels turn at different speeds in a corner. It only limits how far apart they can go.

A locking differential forces both wheels on an axle to turn together regardless of grip. According to Wikipedia, it can usually be unlocked for normal driving and is mostly found on off-road vehicles. Locked wheels cannot follow different paths in a bend on a hard surface, so the unlocked mode is used for everyday driving.
Brakes can imitate a limited-slip effect

Motor1 adds that many modern cars with open differentials use the brakes on a slipping wheel to copy what an LSD does. Braking the spinning wheel makes it harder to turn, so more torque can pass to the wheel that is gripping.
Not only for the rear axle

Cars with all-wheel drive often have a differential between the front and rear axles as well, since those axles also travel different distances in a turn. Gear Patrol notes that a locking centre differential forces the front and rear axles to turn at the same speed, while the individual wheels can still turn at different speeds if they have open or limited-slip differentials.

Gear trains of this kind are old. Wikipedia says the earliest verified use of a differential is in Joseph Williamson's clock of 1720, and notes that a differential may have been used in the ancient Greek Antikythera mechanism, with the dates given as about 100 BC or about 80 BC. For vehicles, it lists Onésiphore Pecqueur, who included a differential on the driven rear axle in a steam wagon patent of 1827, and James Starley, who patented one for a quadricycle in 1876. Carl Benz built one into his Patent-Motorwagen in 1885.
This article describes how differentials work in general. Designs vary by manufacturer and vehicle, so refer to the owner's manual for a specific car.

Cornering makes the outer wheel travel farther than the inner one.
A differential lets the two driven wheels turn at different speeds.
An open differential is simple but sends torque to the wheel with less grip.
Limited-slip designs reduce that problem.
Locking differentials force both wheels together and are mostly for off-road use.

sources.title: What is a limited-slip differential?, Motor1

articles.title: The Citroën 2CV: An Umbrella on Four Wheels, 1948 to 1990
articles.excerpt: Citroën set out to build a cheap, tough car for farmers and showed the 2CV in 1948. It stayed in production for 42 years. Here is how it came about and ended.
blocks: The Citroën 2CV was a small, cheap, simple French car that went on show at the Paris Salon on 7 October 1948 and stayed in production until 27 July 1990. It was designed around the needs of people in the countryside, with a soft long-travel suspension, a small air-cooled engine and a body built to be light and practical. More than five million were sold, depending on how a count is made.

According to Wikipedia, a Citroën market survey in the mid-1930s led to a brief for an inexpensive and rugged car described as an umbrella on four wheels. It was to carry four people and 50 kg of farm goods at 50 km/h, use no more than 3 litres of fuel per 100 km, and let the driver cross a ploughed field with a basket of eggs unbroken. Pierre-Jules Boulanger, then head of the company, sent the brief to the design team in 1936.
The original name was TPV, short for Toute Petite Voiture, meaning very small car. The Drive reports that about 250 trial cars with water-cooled engines were built over the next three years.

A launch had been planned for 1939, but Wikipedia says the outbreak of war cancelled it. The Drive adds that the Michelin family, who owned Citroën, hid the prototypes from German forces after the occupation of France in 1940. The car that appeared in 1948 was reworked from the TPV. Sources differ on exactly when series production began, with some suggesting 1948 and others mid-1949.

**Engine:** the first car had a 375 cc air-cooled flat-twin rated at 6.6 kW (9 hp). Later versions used 425 cc, 602 cc and, from 1970, an updated 435 cc engine, according to Wikipedia.
**Suspension:** long-travel springs linked front and rear wheels, which gave a soft ride and helped keep the body level over bumps.
**Body and seats:** The Drive describes removable seating, and a design aimed at rough ground.
Because the engine was air-cooled, it had no radiator or coolant to look after. The car was designed to be simple to repair and to run on little fuel.
From car to family of vehicles
The 2CV platform was reused for other models. Wikipedia names the Ami, Dyane, Acadiane and Méhari among the derivatives. The Drive notes that vans and pickups used the same underpinnings.

Counts vary with what is included. Wikipedia gives about 3.8 million 2CVs and over 9 million vehicles once derivatives are added. The Drive says Citroën sold more than 5.1 million 2CVs, and that the platform's underpinnings went into nearly 9 million vehicles in all. One search result for the last car's number gave 5,114,961, while another source gave 5,114,969, so the exact final figure is not settled. Treat all these numbers as approximate and dependent on whether vans are counted.

French production ended in 1988 at the Levallois-Perret plant, and Wikipedia gives the date of the last French-built car as 25 February. Production continued in Mangualde, Portugal. The last car was finished there on 27 July 1990, and The Drive says it was a two-tone grey 2CV 6 Charleston built for the plant manager, with a marching band marking the occasion. The same article says series production had run for 42 years across 11 plants. Reasons reported for the end include stricter exhaust and safety rules that the design could no longer meet.
Sources agree on 27 July 1990 for the last car, but differ on production totals and on when series production began. This article gives the ranges rather than choosing one figure.

1936: the brief is sent to the design team.
1939: planned launch cancelled by war.
7 October 1948: the car is shown at the Paris Salon.
1970: updated 435 cc engine introduced.
25 February 1988: last French-built car at Levallois-Perret.
27 July 1990: last car completed in Mangualde, Portugal.

The 2CV is remembered because the design brief was followed so closely, and because the car stayed in production for 42 years with limited change. The brief called for low cost, low fuel use and ride comfort on bad roads, and the car's long-travel suspension and small engine were direct answers to those aims.

sources.title: The Final Citroen 2CV Was Built on This Day in 1990, The Drive
